title: Platform gameday exercise automation and scripting playbook
author: Diego Morales
body:
Summary:
This playbook defines a repeatable, automatable process for running platform-level gamedays (simulated incidents and load exercises). It covers exercise types, preconditions, scripting templates, dashboard and alert validation, automated injection tooling, roles & responsibilities, and a post-exercise triage that feeds back into runbook and dashboard improvements. The goal is to increase runbook coverage, reduce mean time to detect/acknowledge/resolve, and validate graceful degradation strategies across Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployment modes.

Scope:
- Applies to platform-level services and infra components owned by Eng Platform (routing, service discovery, autoscaler, model serving mesh, cost-metering).
- Includes integration points: alerting (PagerDuty/Slack), observability (Grafana/Prometheus/Tempo), chaos tooling (ChaosMesh, kube-perturb), and CI pipelines that provision ephemeral environments.
- Excludes application-level functional tests owned by product teams (those teams should coordinate their own gamedays and share results).

Goals and Success Criteria:
- Validate at least one rollback/fallback path for each critical service during the exercise.
- Reduce average time-to-identify (TTI) for simulated 99th-percentile latency incidents by 25% within 3 exercises.
- Ensure all alerts exercised fire with correct severity and runbook link metadata.
- Produce a prioritized remediation list and close >= 50% of P1 follow-ups within 30 days.

Exercise Types (choose one or combine):
1) Degradation: Introduce increased latency or partial request loss to a target service (simulate high concurrency).
2) Resource Exhaustion: Saturate GPU/CPU or disk to validate autoscaler and eviction policies.
3) Control Plane Failure: Disable orchestration layer components (e.g., controller-manager replica) to test self-healing and operator runbooks.
4) Routing/Network Partition: Block cross-region traffic or specific subnets to validate multi-region fallbacks.
5) Canary Failure Mode: Force a canary model to serve bad outputs to validate automatic rollback and quality gates.
6) Cost Spike: Synthetic workload that produces unexpected token volume to validate quota and alerting pipelines.

Preconditions and Safety Checks (required before any automated injection):
- Executive sign-off for customer-impacting exercises recorded in the exercise ticket.
- A maintenance window or explicit blackout list created for high-risk customers.
- Automated smoke test harness that runs pre- and post-exercise: health-check endpoints for all involved services must return OK.
- Backup rollback plan and contact list for on-call owners.
- Throttle limits set in injection tooling to cap incident severity.

Roles & Responsibilities:
- Exercise Lead (owner_team: engineering): prepares script, coordinates calendar and stakeholders, tracks goals.
- Incident Commander (rotating oncall): drives response during the exercise and records timelines.
- Observability Owner: ensures dashboards/alerts are instrumented, adjusts sampling/retention for the exercise.
- SRE/Platform Engineers: execute injection scripts and perform mitigation steps.
- Product/Customer Ops (optional): observe customer-facing impacts and validate communication templates.

Script Template (canonical, editable example):
- Metadata: title, start_time, expected_impact_level (low/medium/high), services_targeted, rollback_plan, throttle_limit.
- Phases:
  1. Baseline collection: 60s metrics snapshot + tracing baseline for target services.
  2. Inject (t=0): apply fault with throttle_limit.
  3. Observe (t=0..t+N): monitor SLOs, alert firing, logs and traces.
  4. Escalate (if defined thresholds are reached): page incident commander.
  5. Recover: execute rollback or mitigation path from runbook.
  6. Post-check: run smoke tests and validate all metrics returned to baseline.
- Example YAML snippet: 
  ---
  title: "gameday: model-serving-latency-degradation"
  start_time: "2026-03-10T14:00:00Z"
  expected_impact_level: "medium"
  services_targeted: ["model-proxy", "kv-cache-service"]
  throttle_limit: 0.35  # 35% of traffic
  rollback_plan: "disable-injection; revert-proxy-config; scale-up-cache"

Runbook: Execution checklist (step-by-step)
1) Pre-run (72-24 hours out):
   - Create an exercise ticket including scope, safety list, and communication plan.
   - Notify customer success and legal if the exercise touches restricted customers.
   - Verify chaos tooling credentials and that scripts are in the exercise repo.
   - Ensure alert paging destinations are configured for the simulation channel.
2) Day-of (T-60 to T0):
   - Run baseline smoke tests and collect metrics.
   - Snapshot current autoscaler policies and deployment manifests.
   - Confirm oncall rotation and primary/secondary contacts.
3) During run (T0 to T+N):
   - Start injection at throttle_limit; monitor dashboards.
   - Incident Commander documents timeline and decisions in the exercise ticket.
   - If an alert is expected but does not fire within configured alert-sla (default 3 mins), pause injection and escalate to Observability Owner.
4) Recovery (T_recover):
   - Follow the documented rollback steps.
   - Validate service health and run smoke tests.
5) Immediate Post-check (T+30m):
   - Confirm no lingering paging noise and that costs/log volume returned to baseline projections.
6) Postmortem & Remediation (within 7 days):
   - Complete a lightweight postmortem template and categorize findings: instrumentation gaps, runbook gaps, orchestration gaps, human process gaps.
   - Assign remediation owners with deadlines.

Alerting & Dashboard Validation Checklist:
- For each alert exercised, ensure:
  - Alert includes runbook link and severity.
  - PagerDuty rotation for service matches current oncall roster.
  - Grafana panel shows expected metric and time window.
- Dashboard checklist table (copy into new exercise ticket):
  Metric | Expected change | Alert to exercise | Panel to observe | Owner
  -- | -- | -- | -- | --
  model_latency_p95 | +30% | latency-critical | model-serving/p95-panel | @sre-modeling
  kv_cache_hitrate | -20% | cache-warning | cache/hitrate | @infra-cache
  token_throughput | +50% | cost-alert | billing/token-rate | @billing

Failure Injection Matrix (example):
- Latency bump: inject delay in model-proxy (50–250ms) at slice sizes 10–50% of traffic.
- Partial error: return HTTP 503 from a single replica; validate routing fallback.
- Total node kill: drain and kill a node running critical controller to test leader election.
- Disk pressure: fill ephemeral disk to 85% and observe eviction and pod rescheduling behavior.

Automation patterns and CI integration:
- Store canonical scripts in the platform-exercises repo under /exercises/{year}/{service}.
- CI job that validates the script syntax, runs static safety checks, and schedules a dry-run in a sandbox cluster.
- Use feature-flagged automation: real injections require a two-step approval (code + ticket approver) recorded in Git and the exercise ticket.
- Terraform/Argo job templates to provision ephemeral stacks for lower-risk exercises.

Observability & Measurement (KPIs to record per exercise):
- Mean Time To Detect (MTTD) — goal: reduce by 25% over 3 exercises.
- Mean Time To Acknowledge (MTTA) — goal: < 3 minutes for P1.
- Mean Time To Resolve (MTTR) — goal: < 45 minutes for simulated P1.
- Runbook hit rate: % of incidents where the runbook was consulted and followed.
- Alert fidelity: % of expected alerts that fired and were actionable.
- False-positive noise: number of unrelated alerts triggered during the exercise.

Postmortem template (to attach to the exercise ticket):
- Title, date, exercise lead, participants.
- Timeline: A clear minute-by-minute log of actions and observations.
- Impact summary: systems affected, customer-visible effects.
- Root cause (as understood), contributing factors.
- Runbook & instrumentation gaps discovered.
- Action items with owners and due dates (link to JIRA epic).
- Retrospective ratings: confidence in recovery path (1-5), coverage completeness (1-5), tooling reliability (1-5).

Common failure modes observed historically:
- Alert thresholds mismatched with traffic baselines, leading to either late or noisy paging.
- Missing runbook links in alert payloads.
- Insufficient throttling in injection scripts causing broader customer impact.
- Canary quality gates not wired into automatic rollback in some dedicated deployments.

Follow-up cadence and roadmap tie-ins:
- Weekly exercise review: the Exercise Lead runs a 30-minute review meeting in the week after an exercise to triage action items.
- Quarterly platform gameday: cross-functional exercise with Product and Customer Ops to validate user-facing fallbacks.
- Roadmap items: prioritize runbook expansion and automated remediation (Remediation-as-Code) as part of the SRE backlog; align with the platform roadmap theme "Operational Resilience" for the next two quarters.

Appendix: Useful commands and snippets
- Run baseline smoke test: curl -sSf https://model-proxy.health/readiness
- Trigger a controlled latency injection (example using kube-perturb CLI):
  kube-perturb inject latency --namespace platform --selector app=model-proxy --latency 200ms --percentage 25 --duration 5m
- Query recent alerts (Prometheus Alertmanager API):
  curl -sS "${ALERTMGR}/api/v2/alerts?receiver=platform-simulation" | jq
- Revert injection: kube-perturb revert --all --confirm

Ownership & contact list:
- Platform SRE Oncall Slack channel: #sre-platform-oncall
- PagerDuty service: SRE-Platform-Primary
- Playbook owner (doc): Diego Morales (diego@redwood.ai)
- Observability owner: Lina Chen (lina@redwood.ai)

End of playbook.
